verses.1: Al-Mizan distinguishes qirāʾah as assembling letters and words in the mind, in spoken recitation, or in another’s hearing; tilāwah can share the last sense. Here iqraʾ apparently commands the Prophet to receive and read the Qur’an from the angel of revelation, although the command is itself part of the book. It therefore indicates the first revealed verses and an omitted object, the Qur’an, rather than a general command, reciting only the divine name, or reading to the people; the last is a wider Qur’anic objective but not this verse’s meaning. Bi-ism is governed either by an implied beginning or by mulābasah, connection and accompaniment, so God begins the sūrah with His name while teaching the Prophet to begin reading with it. ‘Your Lord who created’ restricts both creation and rubūbiyyah—the direction of all beings and their affairs—to God, refuting the polytheist division between a creator God and managing angels, jinn, or humans, and entails worship of Him alone.
verses.2: Al-Mizan takes al-insān as the human genus and ʿalaq as dried blood, the stage into which sperm develops in the womb. God’s successive management from that stage to the completed human being is ceaseless creation and divine oversight. Since no person reaches completion and perfection without it, God is both humanity’s Creator and Lord; people can have no lord besides Him, which establishes the unity of lordship.
verses.3: Al-Mizan says the unqualified second command to Read reiterates and emphasizes the first; interpretations that distinguish private reading from proclamation, or make both commands public proclamation, do not fit the apparent wording. God is ‘the most gracious’ because His giving precedes the recipient’s merit and qualification, and every gift or blessing ultimately derives from Him.
verses.4: Al-Mizan explains teaching by the pen as teaching reading, or reading and writing, through the pen. The verse reassures the unlettered Prophet when commanded to read: the most gracious Lord who taught humanity through the writing instrument can teach him to read the revealed book, and would not command him without enabling him to do so.
verses.5: Al-Mizan sees the verse as extending the stated blessings to God’s teaching humankind what it did not know, thereby strengthening and gladdening the Prophet. Al-insān apparently means humanity as a genus, while identifications with Adam, Idrīs because he first wrote with a pen, or all writing prophets are unfounded and do not arise from the text.
verses.6: Al-Mizan reads kallā as rejecting the implication that human beings should thank God for knowledge, the pen, and revelation: instead they transgress, crossing their limits. Raʾāhu derives from raʾy, opinion, not physical sight, and both its subject and object are al-insān. Transgression follows from judging oneself self-sufficient: absorbed in limited selfhood and material means, people fail to recognize God’s blessings or need of Him, and so neither remember nor thank Him.

verses.8: Al-Mizan identifies al-rujʿá with rujūʿ, return, and in the surrounding threat reads it as a warning of death and resurrection. The address is apparently to the Prophet; the proposed shift to addressing the human being in order to intensify the threat is less apparent.
verses.9: Al-Mizan presents these verses as an instance of human transgression and a prelude to the ensuing threat and command not to obey it. The praying servant is the Prophet; if this sūrah was first and revealed together, that implies he prayed before the Qur’an’s formal commission and hence was a prophet before it. Against the objection that ṣalāh was only mandated at the ascension, the commentary says only the present five-prayer form was then definitively legislated; earlier Meccan references and reports of the Prophet praying with Khadījah and ʿAlī leave earlier prayer possible. ‘Have you seen’ means ‘tell me’ and rhetorically asks what awaits one who forbids a servant’s prayer, especially if that servant is guided or calls to Godwariness, while the forbidder denies and turns away despite the consequences of God’s seeing. The alternative that every pronoun concerns the forbidder is unlikely. The idol-worshiper’s professed belief in God as flawless Creator itself supplied the grounds for knowing that God knows all things.

verses.15: Al-Mizan, citing Majmaʿ al-bayān, defines safʿ as a forceful grasp. ‘Lying, sinful forelock’ metaphorically describes its owner, and the verse vehemently threatens the person who persists in forbidding prayer: he will be seized by the forehead, humiliated, and dragged to the fire as one who denied in speech and sinned in action. It reports an alternative interpretation that the forehead will be burned and blackened by the fire.

verses.17: Al-Mizan explains nādī as a gathering and, apparently, the people assembled there, though it can also mean a companion; al-zabāniyah are the guardian angels of hell, with ‘sentry’ or ‘patrol’ also reported. The command to call his comrades is condescending: the person forbidding worship may summon every friend, but God will summon harsh guardians of hell, against whom no helper can prevail.

verses.19: Al-Mizan treats the repeated Nay as emphasis of the preceding rejection. The Prophet is not to obey the one obstructing prayer, but to prostrate and draw near; iqtirāb means nearness to God, though some take it as advancing toward His reward. Prostration here apparently belongs to prayer, perhaps then centered on glorification and prostration; some exegetes instead identify it with the obligatory prostration after this sūrah, one of the Qur’an’s four such places.
